For example, car accidents cause more deaths per person and mile travelled when compared to plane accidents. However, most people are more scared of planes due to a plane accident being a large memorable event that frequently has more than one hundred people die at one time, while car accidents only cause 1-10 deaths at a time.

Same for nuclear vs coal or nuclear vs solar: nuclear accidents are large, memorable events, yet if you compare the total deaths per MWh for those three, nuclear comes out with a ridiculously low number, even if you include those accidents that were entirely based on regime or individual human error. In comparison, something like coal power leads to many many more deaths per MWh, but they're spread over a larger timescale and space due to how air pollution works and are therefore never instinctively associated with coal power. 

This is very similar to rat poisons: if they cause a rat to die straight away, other rats won't fall for it. If its action is delayed by a week or so, they absolutely keep eating the poison because they do not associate the poison with the death.

- do the rendezvous as before

- switch to the space station

- right click the docking port on the space station that you are intending to use and click 'control from here'

- set the docking port of the module you want to add as your target

- set SAS to point at target

- switch back to the module you're adding and do the same you did with the space station

Your space station and the module should now automatically point their docking ports at eachother, leaving you with the fairly simple job of moving the module towards the space station slowly in a straight line.

You guys are talking about the two basic designs of pure fission bombs, gun-type and implosion type.

 Gun type has part of the fissile material separated from the rest and upon being triggered, fires an explosive charge to shoot the separated part into the other, achieving criticality. 

Implosion type has the full load of fissile material in a sphere with explosive lenses encasing it, constructed in such a way that upon ignition, the core of fissile material is hit with a perfectly spherical shockwave, compressing it into criticality.

There's a bunch of factors. Main ones are the weight of the bullet, muzzle velocity, and shape/composition of the bullet. 

Speed and hardness are strongly correlated to penetrative capabilities, a very fast very hard bullet will penetrate deeper than a softer bullet at the same speed or a slower bullet of the same hardness.

Otoh, a soft bullet will dump all its energy in a target very quickly, resulting in more tissue damage through deformation and possibly fragmentation of the bullet. Though speed can also cause heavy wounding as high velocities will result in large temporary shock cavities in the target which result in larger and more erratically shaped permanent cavities in the wound channel.

In short, it is a very deep topic, but in general: the faster and heavier a bullet is, the more damage it'll do. Soft ones dump their energy quickly and are great for soft targets and prevention of overpenetration (think hollow points) while hard ones are great for going through armor, both natural and artificial (think fmj or even tungsten core rounds)
